A shop and six flats in Málaga’s old town: which half carries the yield?

One prompt, two Casafari connectors, thirteen calls. Claude priced both halves of a mixed-use building near Plaza de la Merced from properties on the market, Location Intelligence and residential market data, and wrote this report.

THE PROMPT

I'm valuing a Málaga building with a 150 m² shop and 6 apartments above, near Plaza de la Merced. Give me the commercial rent per m² for comparable shops in the district (market snapshot plus the nearest comparable premises on the market). Then give me apartment rent per m² within 500 m, with its 2-year trend, time on market and bedroom mix. Estimate the blended gross rent, show which half of the building carries the yield, and flag the risks in each.

The answer

The flats carry the income. The shop carries the yield.

On today’s asking data the building would let for about €13,116 a month, €157,392 a year, against an asking value of about €2.73m.

The six flats bring in 82% of the rent and hold 87% of the value. The shop earns 8.1% gross against 5.4% for the flats, because the old town prices shops far below homes per square metre. Both halves have room to run: the nearest shops on the market ask €27.7/m² against the €16.0 district median used here, and apartment rents within 500 m are up 10% on the year before.

What to watch

Risks in each half

The shop

  • Most nearby shops change hands as business transfers, so tenants pay key money and turn over often.
  • Shops take about 165 days to let in Málaga: budget a long void between tenants.
  • More than half the footfall comes from visitors, which ties the tenant’s trade to tourism.
  • Retail rents rose 1.4% in a year while prices rose 6.9%: commercial yields are compressing.

The flats

  • Rents swing with the season, from €24 to €39/m² within a year, a sign of short lets in the mix.
  • Check tourist-licence and rent rules for the building before counting on short-let income.
  • Larger flats above €2,000 a month take up to three and a half months to let.
  • Prices are rising faster than rents, so residential yields are thinning.
